items.title: Davis Furniture and jehs+laub Introduce the Sculptural Laken Nesting Tables
items.summary:
Three steel parts shape the silhouette of the Laken Occasional Table Series : a spun cone settling low against the floor, a slender column drawing upward from its center, and a second cone opening wide to cradle a circular top. The dual-cone composition gives jehs+laub ’s design for Davis Furniture its distinctly modern profile, extended to a set of three nesting tables.

Designed to nest seamlessly or stand alone, the three round tables scale from a single grouping to individual pieces. Image courtesy of Davis Furniture.

Laken continues a collaboration between Davis and jehs+laub that began in 2009, and it carries forward the studio’s approach to balancing soft curvature with precise, architectural form. On every Laken table, gentle radii and careful proportions ease the move from flared base to slender column to inverted cone, and each piece appears fully resolved from any angle.

Nested together or used on their own, the tables can be layered into a single, dynamic arrangement or spread throughout an interior, adapting to lounge, hospitality, and collaborative environments.

Each round tabletop is supported by an inverted steel cone. Image courtesy of Davis Furniture.

The sculptural form belies a carefully engineered base. Its spun steel cones and steel column are mechanically fastened through concealed hardware for a tight, durable assembly built to perform over time, and a ballast hidden within the lower cone brings the center of gravity down, giving the tables stability and resistance to tipping.

Available in three sizes, Laken Tables offer a wide range of…
items.t: Davis Furniture and jehs+laub Introduce the Sculptural Laken Nesting Tables

items.title: "Intensely physical patterns" cloak Gerhard Richter's self-designed gallery in Doha
items.summary:
Kaleidoscopic patterns adorn the exterior of this pavilion in Doha, Qatar, designed by artist Gerhard Richter with US studio Selldorf Architects as an art gallery. 

Simply called Doha Pavilion, the psychedelic structure was conceived a work of both art and architecture for MIA Park – a public space outside the Museum of Islamic Art by IM Pei .

Photographs 

Previous 

Next 

Photographs

Close 

It serves as a permanent pavilion for the site and as a gallery for Richter's own work.

Richter designed the Doha Pavilion with Selldorf Architects as a reference to his Strip paintings – a series that involved digitally dividing his Abstract Painting artwork into vertical stripes, building on his earlier explorations of colour, pattern and repetition.

"My trip to Doha in 2013 came two years into developing my Strip paintings, and the city’s architecture and history sparked an idea for a pavilion that could unite the thematic threads of that body of work," said Richter.

"The pavilion’s exterior features decorative tiles based on the patterns that first led me to the Strips," he continued. "Doha is the right place and the only place for my pavilion.”

Doha Pavilion has a six-sided form, wrapped in psychedelic tiles displaying repeating, kaleidoscopic patterns that recall geometries seen in Islamic art, nodding to the project's context.

Selldorf Architects founder Annabelle Selldorf said the design reflects a "profound culmination of many years of [Richter's] research into abstraction".

items.t: "Intensely physical patterns" cloak Gerhard Richter's self-designed gallery in Doha

items.title: Meet Courage Dzidula Kpodo, Lesley Lokko's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years
items.summary:
Ghanaian-Scottish architect Lesley Lokko has nominated Courage Dzidula Kpodo as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler .

In this interview he explains why despite growing global attention, his ambitions remain resolutely local.

Having only graduated in 2025 from a master’s in architecture at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) – for which he was awarded the Arthur Rotch Prize for highest overall mark – Kpodo is already someone Lokko believes will "help shape the next chapter of African architecture".

Kpodo’s work, which sees him blur the roles of architect, artist and archivist, is focused on revealing what he calls the “silences” in prevailing narratives about Ghanaian architecture, and challenging the idea that Ghana’s future development must be a "linear prescription of urbanisation".

If this sounds theoretical or speculative, Kpodo’s approach is anything but: the site of his MIT thesis was an almost five-acre stretch of farmland in Ghana to which he purchased a 99-year lease in 2022, and is currently using as a live site to consider alternative forms of development in the region.

Lesley Lokko (above) has selected Courage Dzidula Kpodo for Dezeen's 20x20 project. Photo by Festus Jackson Davis. 

Stating how, if nothing else, the purchase would "preserve the value of the money I had in my savings account," Kpodo sees the site becoming an alternative institution of sorts, constructed using materials he has salvaged from vernacular buildings that would otherwise be demolished.

“The committee at MIT…
items.t: Meet Courage Dzidula Kpodo, Lesley Lokko's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

items.title: Biscuit-tin lids, horse brasses and scrap metal form sculptural V&A Christmas tree by Burberry
items.summary:
Fashion brand Burberry 's chief creative officer Daniel Lee worked with artist Ann Carrington to create a Christmas tree sculpture for the Victoria & Albert Museum , made from "memories, traditions and little treasures."

The 16-foot (4.8-metre) tree, which was unveiled this week, sits in the entrance hall of the Victoria & Albert Museum (VA's) South Kensington location and was designed to celebrate craft and creativity.

"This collaboration with Ann is a celebration of creativity and what better place to showcase this than the V&A?" Lee said. "It’s one of my favourite museums and a constant source of inspiration to me."

Lee and Carrington made the tree from old money boxes, biscuit and sweet-tin lids, trinket dishes, silver trays, horse brasses and embossed plates, which were turned into rosettes and ribbons and attached to a metal frame.

The tree, which was made as part of Burberry 's 170th anniversary celebrations, also features ribbons and bows made of scrap metal.

According to Lee, he and Carrington made the sculpture from "memories, traditions and little treasures. Objects and materials that most people would overlook."

Read:

Burberry unveils "archive-inspired" charging knight logo 

Carrington added that the design was inspired by the ritual of getting old Christmas decorations out of storage in time for the festive season.

"We wanted to capture that magical moment when you retrieve the battered old box of Christmas decorations from the loft, sift through the faded party bows and tattered tinsel accumulated through the generations and begin the joyful ritual…
items.t: Biscuit-tin lids, horse brasses and scrap metal form sculptural V&A Christmas tree by Burberry

items.title: ‘An extravagantly illuminated beast’: the best artificial Christmas trees in the UK – tested

• The best beauty Advent calendars

In the 70s and 80s Essex of my youth, no one had a real Christmas tree unless they lived in the country, or perhaps Loughton. Our family’s skinny artificial tree is now 55 years old and comes out every year at my sister’s. It’s shed a few plastic “needles” down the years, but it’s still standing proud – which is more than you can say for a real Christmas tree bought in 1971, or even 2025.

Therein lies the surprising environmental efficiency of artificial Christmas trees. The Carbon Trust says using a fake tree over seven to 20 years (depending on its weight and materials) can create fewer emissions than buying a new, commercially grown tree every year. The key is to buy an artificial tree you’ll love enough to roll out for decades.

items.title: Five key projects by Dezeen Awards emerging architect of the year Kuma&Elsa
items.summary:
This year Kuma&Elsa was named emerging architect of the year at the Dezeen Awards . Here, they select five projects that demonstrate the ethos of the studio.

Led by Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French-Spanish urban designer Elsa Escobedo, Kuma&Elsa has completed a wide variety of projects from their bases in France and Japan.

"We believe it is important not to impose a common consistency across our projects," Kuma told Dezeen. 

"Every project is unique, shaped by a one-off combination of site and client. Preserving that uniqueness requires an open mind. Personally, I quickly lose interest when things are planned in advance."

"That said, there are certain topics, many of which are shared by our generation, such as feminism, the care for natural resources and a shared public space, that interest us on a personal level, and I imagine they find their way into our work," added Escobedo. 

Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo lead Dezeen Award-winning studio Kuma&Elsa 

"We try to approach them with a sense of joy."

Although they have already designed a wide range of projects, from installations to houses and public toilets, the duo would like to work on more varied schemes and unusual projects, along with completing their own, long-running renovation.

"It would be nice to actually finish this self-renovation project at some point..." said Escobedo. 

"More seriously, I'd love to experiment with the reuse of materials on a larger scale, or in a European context, working with European craftspeople."

"I would love to work on overlooked building types and uses, especially…
items.t: Five key projects by Dezeen Awards emerging architect of the year Kuma&Elsa

items.summary:
Architecture studios Stanton Williams , Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects have completed their long-awaited transformation of the 1880s Smithfield General Market into the London Museum.

Opening to the public on Saturday, the former Victorian market hall now functions as a museum that tells the story of London's history through exhibitions designed by German studio Atelier Brückner .

According to the London Museum , it is the largest dedicated city museum in the world.

The London Museum is opening this weekend

Ten years in the making, the opening of Smithfield General Market marks the first phase of the London Museum's relocation from the Barbican Estate's former Museum of London, which is set to be demolished .

Stanton Williams , Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects have overhauled the General Market, which fell into disrepair after it closed in the 1990s, and will also convert the adjacent 1960s Poultry Market , which is expected to open in 2028.

A covered street forms the museum entrance 

"There's an opportunity to represent London as it is now and in the future, and really take city museums to another level," said London Museum's New Museum Project director Alec Shaw.

"We're bringing back a bit of London's heritage – one building that has not been seen or encountered for at least 30 years, and the other one an amazing architectural gem that hasn't been fully appreciated and will now be," he told Dezeen.

items.summary:
Spanish studio Raúl Sánchez Architects turned a former washhouse into Casa de las Lavanderas, with a lightwell that is a "modern translation of the old wells" used by local laundry workers.

The home is located on Barcelona's picturesque Calle Aiguafreda street, historically an area where washerwomen used wells to handwash their clients' clothes.

The house is now home to a couple and their newborn baby.

The lower level of the 80-square-metre building was partly underground and very dark, leading the studio to look for new solutions to add more light.

"Since the ground floor is semi-basement, the area furthest from Aiguafreda Street was darker, so to bring light into it, I incorporated this lightwell topped with a skylight," studio founder Rául Sánchez told Dezeen.

The lightwell also functions as a "modern translation of the old wells" that used to provide water for the laundry workers.

Casa de las Lavanderas faces two streets – Calle Aiguafreda and Calle Granollers – and has entrances on both sides, with the Calle Aiguafreda entrance sitting 1.5 metres lower than that on Calle Granollers.

From here, one flight of stairs leads down to the lower level and the Calle Aiguafreda entrance, and another up to the house's upper level.

The hall's glazed interior was illuminated and washed in vivid colours drawn from this year's awards graphic identity in a show design led by Hingston Studio .

Partygoers enjoyed their drinks set against a textile softwall bar backdrop designed by Stephanie Forsythe and Todd MacAllen for Canadian studio Molo , known for its sculptural space partitions, furniture and lighting made from paper and textile.

Guests gathered and networked ahead of the evening's highly anticipated announcements

items.title: Mason & Fifth's Belsize Park guesthouse was designed to be “domestic and low-impact”
items.summary:
Design studio Holloway Li has collaborated with architecture practice New-works to conceive the interiors of this London apartment hotel , incorporating circular features meant to stand the test of time.

Mason & Fifth guesthouses are composed of fully furnished private apartments where guests have the flexibility of staying anywhere from one night to several months at a time.

The company has three sites across London, with one in Primrose Hill, another in Westbourne Park, and now Belsize Park.

The Belsize Park location occupies Ornan Court, a 19th-century mansion block that once formed part of the Ivy Bank residential estate. 

Architecture practice New-works adapted the building for hospitality use, establishing a series of communal spaces at ground level that could serve as a social hub for guests.

At its heart is a large shared kitchen, centred by a chunky tiled breakfast island, followed by a lounge area with intimate groupings of timber-frame chairs and two khaki-coloured sofas, complementing the glossy green fireplace.

items.title: Fireclay Tile Turns Traditional Textiles Into Hand-Painted Tile
items.summary:
Plaids and florals might seem more at home on upholstery or wallpaper than ceramic tile, but Fireclay Tile’s latest collection makes a compelling case for bringing those familiar patterns to harder surfaces. Called Idyllwild, the new hand-painted collection takes inspiration from traditional textiles, translating everything from delicate botanical illustrations to richly layered plaids into ceramic designs that feel both nostalgic and contemporary.

Interestingly, the collection didn’t begin with flowers at all. “We were seeing designers use a lot of intricate textiles, colors, and patterns together,” explains Jamie Chappell, VP of Brand and Product at Fireclay Tile, adding that early explorations focused on plaids and stripes. “As a true lover of ’90s alt-rock, I actually went down a rabbit hole early on, wondering if it should be a ‘grunge’ collection.”

Fireclay Tile’s Idyllwild collection in its Winter palette, featuring deep blues, earthy greens, and warm neutrals across floral, striped, and plaid patterns.

That direction eventually gave way to something softer. Recognizing the longstanding relationship between florals and plaids in interiors, the team introduced botanical patterns to balance the collection’s more structured designs. The name Idyllwild followed, referencing the California mountain town.

The resulting collection includes 16 patterns organized into four categories: Specimen Flowers, Idyllwild Florals, Idyllwild Stripes, and Idyllwild Plaids.

The Specimen Flowers series features four individual botanical motifs—Allium, Carnation, Lily, and…

items.title: Art Meets the Slopes at Powder Mountain’s Outdoor Gallery
items.summary:
Most skiers and snowboarders will likely pause at some point during a day on the slopes to take in their surroundings. After all, ski resorts typically offer great mountain views. But at Powder Mountain in Utah, visitors get more than a scenic view. They might also encounter a bright pink pineapple rising among the pines, a classical Greek column twisted into an improbable shape, or poetry carved into a boulder. These three installations are the latest additions to Powder Art Foundation ’s skiable outdoor art museum, an evolving collection that challenges how—and where—we experience art.

Davina Semo’s Listener (2020–2024), a patinated cast-bronze bell, is part of Powder Art Foundation’s outdoor art collection at Utah’s Powder Mountain. Photography courtesy of Powder Art Foundation.

Established in 2024 in partnership with Dia Art Foundation , Powder Art Foundation occupies 8,000 acres of Utah’s Wasatch Mountains. The foundation’s goal is to bring contemporary installations into dialogue with the landscape while honoring the region’s connection to the Land Art movement.

“We’re building a collection that people encounter while spending time outdoors, so I’m interested in work that can surprise you and hold your attention without needing a museum around it,” says Alex Zhang, chief creative officer of Powder Mountain.

items.title: Estudio A-G uses colour to update 1960s book-lined house in Mexico City
items.summary:
Local studio Estudio A-G has foregrounded a sculptural timber structural element while implementing bold colours for the renovation of a 1960s house in Mexico City.

Originally built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio, Casa Magnolia is located in the residential neighbourhood of San Ángel.

Monasterio designed the home as a domestic library for his brother, who was an avid reader and book collector. Over the decades, the house was renovated multiple times, obscuring the home's original character.

In 2025, Andrés Gutiérrez, head of Estudio A-G , was commissioned to reinterpret the interior of the 275-square-metre residence for new inhabitants, preserving the architectural qualities that made the original design unique.

"Quite the opposite – once restored, the house needed to feel completely new, fresh and contemporary, which was exactly what the clients were looking for."

items.title: Meet AMAA, Neri&Hu’s pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years
items.summary:
An innovative approach to the reuse of existing buildings defines the output of Italian architecture office AMAA, which Neri&Hu has selected as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design as part of Dezeen's 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler .

Led by Marcello Galiotto and Alessandra Rampazzo, over the past 14 years AMAA has become known for its approach to the reuse of post-industrial structures in northern Italy, with the transformation of a former factory building into its own studio , a typical example of its approach.

According to Galiotto, these buildings are a taste of what the studio wants to achieve.

“What we have done in the past 10 years is really just a sketch of what we can do in the future,” he told Dezeen.

“Our research is still growing, and it can be applied to various programmes and contexts,” he continued, “but in 20 years we will both be 60 so we want the studio to be able to evolve and grow in new directions.”

AMAA turned a former factory building into its own studio. Photo by Simone Bossi 

The preservation and adaptation of existing buildings, which is central to AMAA’s practice, is a key reason why architects Lyndon Neri and Rossana Hu selected the studio for Dezeen’s 20x20 series.

"AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse," said the duo, adding that the studio’s ability to repurpose historic structures "positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture".

items.title: RIBA president rejoins ARB register to restore architect title
items.summary:
The president of the Royal Institute of British Architects , Chris Williamson, has decided to renew his membership with the Architects Registration Board , nearly a year after terminating it. 

In a LinkedIn post , Williamson said he was rejoining the Architects Registration Board's (ARB) register because he no longer wanted "to face the prospect of legal action".

Specifically, he said he feared the potential "legal proceedings and financial penalties" from referring to himself as an architect, which ARB does not permit if a person is unregistered.

"I have felt the fear of legal proceedings" 

Williamson's post comes nearly a year after he revealed he was not going to renew his membership to draw attention to what he called the “absurdity of the current regulatory framework” . 

This ARB framework currently only regulates the protected title “architect” and the competence of those on its register, meaning it does not oversee the competence of unregistered providers of architectural services.

His withdrawal from ARB last year aligned with the launch of a campaign by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) calling for a new regulatory model for UK architects.

Read:

RIBA president Chris Williamson to give up architect title 

Though he has now rejoined the ARB register, Williamson said his position on the need to reform remains unchanged.

"Today, I have decided to rejoin the ARB register," he posted on LinkedIn on Friday.

A nine-metre-tall replica of a town hall in Fayetteville, North Carolina, takes centre stage at American rapper J Cole’s world tour set, which has been created by production company Sturdy.

The set for The Fall Off Tour was designed by Los Angeles-based Sturdy to realise J Cole’s ambition to take his hometown, Fayetteville – or "the ville"– "to the world".

To do this, the studio drew on the historic, two-storey Market House building, which has stood as a local landmark in the city since 1832. Sturdy created a weathered, ivy-covered replica of the structure, which is neoclassical with gothic revival details.

“The Market House was chosen because it's an iconic piece of architecture historically as well in the town that J Cole's from,” Martinez told Dezeen. 

“I think a big part of the intention is that he takes home with him wherever he goes; conceptually, the idea was to take ‘the ville’ to the world,” he continued.

“And what better way to do that than something that lives basically at the centre point of the entire city?”

Other nods to the rapper’s life in Fayetteville include the presence of a Honda Civic car, which Martinez describes as a “supporting actor in the show”. 

Positioned in front of the building at centre stage, the car is supported on ties that allow it to be suspended above the stage during specific moments of the performance. 

“The car is like a supporting actor in the show that adds a little bit of an authentic take to the performance,” he said.

items.title: "Sacred" archaeological finds become raw materials for design in Ex Situ exhibition
items.summary:
New objects made from mammoth bone, leather from the middle ages and stumps from a road built under Roman Emperor Hadrian feature in the Ex Situ project, set to be exhibited soon in The Hague .

Initiated and curated by Dutch designer Marisa Klaster , working in concert with archaeologist René Isarin, the project makes use of materials that many in Isarin's profession and the broader public might consider off-limits for new designs: the finds from archaeological digs.

However, while these finds, such as 40,000-year-old mammoth bone and 14th-century ship wood, sound like they belong in a museum, they are in fact deselected – not chosen for inclusion in any archives.

A preview of Ex Situ was shown at Dutch Design Week. Photo by Boudewijn Bollmann 

Deselected finds are duplicates, common in type, poorly preserved or otherwise judged to have limited future research value.

"The material that you see here is the lowest of the lowest quality," said Isarin at a preview of Ex Situ at this year's Dutch Design Week . "It's not preserved. It doesn't belong in a museum. It doesn't belong in a depot."

In fact, if it is not going to be used for educational purposes or reference collections, deselected archaeological finds are required by Dutch law to be carefully destroyed, as they are in many places around the world, said Isarin and Klaster.

Designer Shahar Livne has been working with mammoth bone 

Although the materials may be of low value to archaeology, the designers both found this something of a waste. With Ex Situ, they aim to explore a new category of use and preservation…
items.t: "Sacred" archaeological finds become raw materials for design in Ex Situ exhibition

items.title: Mondaine turns solar technology into design feature with Doppio Solar Skeleton timepiece

Swiss watchmaker Mondaine has expanded its Doppio collection with the Solar Skeleton, a timepiece that brings solar technology into the foreground of its design. 

Rather than concealing the solar plates beneath the dial, the watch reveals them through a precisely cut circular opening, turning a functional component into a defining visual feature.

The Doppio Solar Skeleton reflects Mondaine's commitment to Swiss minimalist design 

The design builds on the distinctive visual language of Mondaine 's Doppio collection, which is characterised by double-line hands and indexes, a concave dial and a double-domed sapphire crystal.

Mondaine explained that these elements establish a sense of repetition, rhythm and structural clarity, while the exposed solar plates introduce an additional layer of depth and visual interest.

The exposed solar plates introduce an additional layer of depth and visual interest 

While solar technology is typically hidden from view, Mondaine has taken a different approach with the Doppio Solar Skeleton. 

A carefully positioned circular opening around the centre of the dial offers a controlled view of the solar movement, while the outer section retains the indexes to ensure clear readability.

By making the technology visible, Mondaine aimed to bridge the watch's technical function with its aesthetic identity, without compromising the "clarity and legibility" that define the collection.

items.title: Domes depict constellations of missiles in the night sky at Sharjah Architecture Triennial

Architect Mohamad Nahleh and architecture professor Ozayr Saloojee have created three domed structures that reimagine constellations by mapping military objects in the night sky, which were displayed at this year's Sharjah Architecture Triennial .

Titled After Night There is Nothing, the trio of installations aim to bring attention to how communities are responding to drones, satellites, rockets and missiles changing the sky above them.

Three domed shells were scattered across locations at the Sharjah Architecture Triennial. Above photo by Edmund Sumner and top photo by Ahmed Osama 

The installation in Al Madam has a vertical cut-out framing a view of a minaret. Photo by Danko Stjepanovic 

Covered in thatch, the three curved wood-and-steel structures are segments of a giant globe.

Vinyl lines the inner curves, where Nahleh and Saloojee designed creature-like constellations based on man-made military objects in the sky.

The trio of installations were displayed at three venues at the Sharjah Architecture Triennial – the Al Qasimiyah School, a former slaughterhouse, and in the sandy Al Madam town.

“This is ‘night sky optimism’ – optimism through catastrophe,” Nahleh told Dezeen. “The night sky we are talking about in this project is not the sky of beautiful stars and constellations, but the contemporary sky filled with drones, satellites, rockets and missiles that are changing the way we understand the sky above us.”

"The drones, missiles, rockets and satellites eclipse some of the constellations, and sometimes fuse with them," he continued.

UK studio ZHA took visual cues from the riverbank site of this national theatre in Morocco when designing its sweeping exterior form, which encases a trio of performance spaces.

Named Théâtre Royal de Rabat, the performance venue for artists and musicians is located between the cities of Rabat and Salé near to the recently completed Mohammed VI Tower, which is the country's tallest building.

It is the first project completed by ZHA , formerly Zaha Hadid Architects, in Africa. 

Photographs 

Previous 

Next

ZHA revealed its proposal for Théâtre Royal de Rabat in 2010 . At the time, the studio’s founder, Zaha Hadid, described the design as “secular”.

"It is uplifting to go into a great space, a heavenly space,” Hadid said.

“As a performance venue, the Théâtre Royal de Rabat is secular, but it has the capacity to transport the audience to an imaginary space and time."

Théâtre Royal de Rabat’s design draws on the topography of its site on the banks of the Bouregreg River, which runs between the two cities.

More than 460 stepped platforms are arranged on top of Prestige University in Indore, Madhya Pradesh, which was recently crowned education project of the year at the 2026 Dezeen Awards.

Its 9,000-square-metre walkable roof gradually steps up from the ground to its full height of 28 metres, reducing the visual heft of the building while providing gathering space for all of the university 's 3,000 students at the same time.

Drawing on the ancient tradition of Indian stepwells, the staircases are organised around courtyards that help to draw sun and ventilation deep into the building, reducing its dependence on artificial light and air conditioning.

items.title: A Brooklyn Exhibition Rethinks the Art of the Candleholder
items.summary:
A candleholder has a relatively simple job: keep a candle upright. Beyond that, the possibilities are nearly endless. At Piscina , a contemporary collectible design gallery in Brooklyn’s Red Hook neighborhood, approximately 80 artists and designers have taken that freedom to heart, creating their own interpretations of the everyday object for a new group exhibition.

An installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

Titled Candelabra Palaver , the exhibition opened Nov. 14, bringing together works selected through an open call. The brief was deliberately straightforward: make an object that holds a candle. With no prescribed materials, proportions, or aesthetic direction, participants could approach the assignment through their individual practices.

An installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

The results explore just how much variation can emerge from a single functional requirement. Some contributors adhere to the familiar conventions of the candelabrum, while others push the object toward sculpture. Across the exhibition, differences in material, scale, and form reveal the many ways designers can interpret an object whose purpose has remained largely unchanged for centuries.

Candelabra by Fort Standard, featured in ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn. Photography courtesy of the artist and Piscina.

items.title: 6 Things I Learned While Hosting ‘The Design Drop’ Podcast
items.summary:
When we launched The Design Drop , the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear. Not the polished success stories or the advice you’ve heard a hundred times, but the mistakes, detours, and unspoken rules that don’t come with a job description.

As futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group , I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals. So getting to sit down with designers, industry leaders, and a few unexpected voices to talk about what they’ve learned along the way? Pretty much my dream job.

What I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself . About careers, confidence, taking risks, and, yes, microphone stands.

After six episodes, here are the biggest lessons I’m taking away from my first season hosting The Design Drop podcast.

1. You don’t have to know what you’re doing to get started. 
 When I talked to furniture designer Nicolai Czumaj-Bront , he shared how his career began at his kitchen table, after long days working as a consultant. No fancy studio or a perfectly mapped-out plan. Just an idea, enough confidence to try it, and a willingness to invest in himself.

Twenty years later, he’s a senior design studio manager at Haworth .

We spend so much time waiting until we feel qualified, prepared, or experienced enough to do something. But how are we supposed to get that experience if we never start? I’m trying to remind myself of this more often, especially when something feels outside my comfort zone.

Listen to Nicolai Czumaj-Bront’s full episode of The…

California-based studio Atelier Manferdini has created an expressive facade system for an electrical substation in Virginia , USA, using metal and colourful tile to represent the flow of electrical power within. 

Called InVisible, the project was carried out for Dominion Energy, an electricity provider that was updating the substation in Crystal City, Northern Virginia, just outside of Washington DC.

Photo by Coulter D Toatley IV

Photo by Coulter D Toatley IV

Photo by Coulter D Toatley IV

Atelier Manferdini founder Elena Manferdini, who is Italian and teaches at Sci-Arc in Los Angeles, said that her studio sought to translate the largely functional structure into something more human.

"Critical infrastructure is essential to our cities, yet the Dominion Energy substation is fundamentally designed for machines rather than people," Manferdini told Dezeen. 

"With inVisible, we wanted to explore this dichotomy, transforming a purely functional structure into something meaningful to the surrounding community," she continued.

"While the interior responds to the needs of machines, the exterior becomes an opportunity to engage with people through color, pattern, and perception, creating a dialogue between infrastructure and the human scale of the city."

The substation converts power into different voltages to facilitate the transmission of energy, and the patterns on the sculptural facade were computationally designed to represent that process.

items.title: Friday Five With Sarah Meyohas: Art, Science, and AI in ‘Phase Transition’
items.summary:
Conceptual artist and technologist Sarah Meyohas explores the intersections of art, science, and finance, translating complex systems into visual experiences. Her work examines how emerging technologies challenge our understanding of intelligence, agency, and the boundaries between living and artificial systems.

In 2015, Meyohas launched Bitchcoin , a cryptocurrency tied to ownership of her physical artwork. An early experiment in blockchain-based art ownership, the project preceded Ethereum’s launch by several months.

Meyohas’s practice draws on the concept of Gesamtkunstwerk , a German term meaning “total work of art,” in which multiple disciplines form a unified whole. Her interest in this approach deepened through conversations with scientists whose research challenged familiar distinctions between the biological and the technological. “Learning about their work consistently evoked a feeling that our categories of life, computation, intelligence, and agency were becoming increasingly unstable,” she explains.

‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, New York.

A Manhattan native with a B.A. in international relations from the University of Pennsylvania and a B.S. in finance from the Wharton School, Meyohas later earned an MFA from Yale. Named to Forbes’ 30 Under 30 list, she has exhibited at the Centre Pompidou in Paris, the ICA in London, and the New Museum in New York. Beyond her studio practice, she invests in companies that reflect her ethical and aesthetic interests, including Sita Bio , which develops…

items.title: CAN combines eclectic references for eccentric revamp of London house
items.summary:
Towers of concrete drainage tubes and colourful exposed steel elements are among the eclectic features of House Tropicália, a “very personal” London residence recently extended by local architecture studio CAN .

Located in Catford, the project responds to a brief with “two distinct strands” – one relating to the functional elements of the project, and the other to its expressive and atmospheric qualities.

Drawings and exterior photos 

Previous 

Next 

Drawings and exterior photos

Close 

Ground floor plan

First floor plan

Functionally, CAN was asked to introduce a new kitchen and dining space that felt connected to the garden, alongside two new bedrooms on the first floor. 

Meanwhile, the design was required to be an expression of the interests and experiences of its clients – designer Fabiane Lee-Perrella, television producer Robin Lee-Perrella and their two sons. 

“The atmospheric side of the brief was to somehow encapsulate the clients' diverse visual tastes and architectural memories from their pasts,” CAN founder Mat Barnes told Dezeen.

“This resulted in the eclecticism of the project; one that is very personal to the clients.”

Visual references given to CAN included modernist Brazilian architecture projects such as Lina Bo Bardi ’s SESC Pompéia in São Paulo, as well as industrial architecture, David Hockney paintings and Moroccan riads.

The resultant design inspired the project's name, House Tropicália, which nods to the late 1960s Tropicália movement that celebrated bold ideas and rebelled against accepted norms.

items.title: I’m a tech expert and new mum. Here’s what I learned testing 17 baby monitors
items.summary:
Our tech expert and new mum tested 17 monitors for picture quality, battery life and reliability – here’s what she recommends

• The best eco-friendly baby products

Moving my baby into her own room to sleep felt liberating and stressful. She was ready for her own space – but was I ready to let her out of my sight? Well, the first thing I did was buy a video baby monitor, so clearly I wasn’t. But it meant she could sleep peacefully in her new room and I could sneak a reassuring peek from afar whenever I felt the need.

There’s a huge range of baby monitors, from simple audio-only options to sophisticated video models. Some even include wearables or other devices to track a baby’s breathing or heart rate, while others offer AI features to analyse sleep patterns. At their most basic, baby monitors typically consist of a baby unit, which you position near the baby, and a parent unit, which lets you hear and/or see them. With video models, the baby unit is essentially a camera, while the parent unit is a screen. Many are also wifi-enabled, meaning you can connect the monitor to your smartphone and view the live feed through an app instead of using a dedicated parent unit (read on for security advice).

items.title: How Klafs Is Rethinking the Sauna Through Design
items.summary:
The sauna is Finnish. The company reimagining it for contemporary homes and spas is German. Klafs , based in Schwäbisch Hall, Germany, sees no contradiction. Its designers approach the centuries-old ritual through engineering, experimenting with heat, air, and materials. As wellness culture expands, the language surrounding its rituals has become increasingly fluid. In my own friend group, “banya” has become nearly shorthand for any spa visit, though it refers specifically to the Russian-style bathhouse. Klafs, by contrast, brings a distinctly German engineering sensibility to these traditions, asking how far the experience can be pushed.

At Klafs headquarters, where the company’s newest ideas are developed and tested, the tour begins in a two-tiered, glass-enclosed sauna. Our guide, an experienced training manager named Heinrich, speaks to the heater in the corner. “Hey, Klafs,” he says, with the intonation we’ve learned from Alexa and other voice-activated devices. I hadn’t considered the possibility of a smart aufguss guide.

In German, aufguss means “infusion,” or literally “pouring over.” In a wellness context, it refers to a guided sauna ritual, typically involving water poured over hot stones, aromatic infusions, and the circulation of heated air. The practice has helped make sauna-going a communal experience in many North American spas. Klafs’s Vitality Boost, which the company describes as the world’s first personalized heat-waving system, brings elements of that ritual into an automated setting: no towel-spinning guide required, and no need to leave the wooden…
